classification.difficultyReason: Requires general proofs extending all five index laws to integer and fractional indices.

inlines.text: Prove that the index laws hold for integer indices. (Use the laws for positive integer indices.)
For example, the product of powers result can be proved in the following way for negative integer indices.

answer.short:
For non-zero bases, all five laws hold for integer indices: $a^ma^n=a^{m+n}$, $\frac{a^m}{a^n}=a^{m-n}$, $(a^m)^n=a^{mn}$, $(ab)^n=a^nb^n$ and $(\frac{a}{b})^n=\frac{a^n}{b^n}$.

Use positive-integer laws, $a^0=1$ and $a^{-k}=\frac{1}{a^k}$, including mixed-sign cases.
answer.worked:
Let $a,b\ne0$. Positive-index cases are already known. The displayed example proves the product law when both indices are negative. If either index is zero, the product law follows from $a^0=1$.

For mixed signs, let $p,q$ be positive integers. If $p>q$, positive-index factorisation gives
$$\begin{align*}a^pa^{-q}&=\frac{a^p}{a^q}\\a^pa^{-q}&=\frac{a^{p-q}a^q}{a^q}\\a^pa^{-q}&=a^{p-q}.\end{align*}$$
If $p=q$, the product is $1=a^0$. If $p<q$,
$$\begin{align*}a^pa^{-q}&=\frac{a^p}{a^pa^{q-p}}\\a^pa^{-q}&=\frac{1}{a^{q-p}}\\a^pa^{-q}&=a^{p-q}.\end{align*}$$
Commutativity covers the opposite order. Thus the product law holds for all integers.

For any integer $n$, the definition of negative powers gives $\frac{1}{a^n}=a^{-n}$. Hence
$$\begin{align*}\frac{a^m}{a^n}&=a^ma^{-n}\\\frac{a^m}{a^n}&=a^{m-n}.\end{align*}$$
For a positive integer $n$, repeated multiplication and the established product law give
$$(a^m)^n=\underbrace{a^m\cdots a^m}_{n\text{ factors}}=a^{mn}.$$
For $n=0$, both sides are $1$. For $n=-q<0$,
$$\begin{align*}(a^m)^{-q}&=\frac{1}{(a^m)^q}\\(a^m)^{-q}&=\frac{1}{a^{mq}}\\(a^m)^{-q}&=a^{-mq}.\end{align*}$$
For positive $n$, the product and quotient power laws are already known; for zero they give $1=1$. For $n=-q<0$,
$$\begin{align*}(ab)^{-q}&=\frac{1}{(ab)^q}\\(ab)^{-q}&=\frac{1}{a^qb^q}\\(ab)^{-q}&=a^{-q}b^{-q},\\\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{-q}&=\frac{1}{(a/b)^q}\\\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{-q}&=\frac{b^q}{a^q}\\\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{-q}&=\frac{a^{-q}}{b^{-q}}.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
All five index laws hold for rational indices with positive bases.

Write the indices over common denominators and use integer laws and the unique positive roots.
answer.worked:
Let $a,b>0$, and write $r=\frac{p}{n}$ and $s=\frac{q}{m}$, where $p,q$ are integers and $n,m$ are positive integers. The definition is $a^{p/n}=(\sqrt[n]{a})^p$, using reciprocals when $p<0$.

First, equivalent fractions define the same power. For a positive integer $k$, put $t=\sqrt[nk]{a}$. Since $(t^k)^n=a$ and $t^k>0$, uniqueness of the positive root gives $t^k=\sqrt[n]{a}$. Consequently $a^{pk/(nk)}=t^{pk}=(\sqrt[n]{a})^p=a^{p/n}$.

Set $x=\sqrt[nm]{a}$. Equivalent fractions and integer laws now give
$$\begin{align*}a^ra^s&=x^{pm}x^{qn}\\a^ra^s&=x^{pm+qn}\\a^ra^s&=a^{\frac{pm+qn}{nm}}\\a^ra^s&=a^{r+s},\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=\frac{x^{pm}}{x^{qn}}\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=x^{pm-qn}\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=a^{\frac{pm-qn}{nm}}\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=a^{r-s}.\end{align*}$$
For the power-of-a-power law, $a^r=x^{pm}$. The positive number $x^p$ satisfies $(x^p)^m=x^{pm}=a^r$, so it is the positive $m$th root of $a^r$. Therefore
$$\begin{align*}(a^r)^s&=(x^p)^q\\(a^r)^s&=x^{pq}\\(a^r)^s&=a^{\frac{pq}{nm}}\\(a^r)^s&=a^{rs}.\end{align*}$$
For the remaining laws, put $u=\sqrt[n]{a}$ and $v=\sqrt[n]{b}$. Integer laws give $(uv)^n=ab$ and $(\frac{u}{v})^n=\frac{a}{b}$. Both $uv$ and $\frac{u}{v}$ are positive, so they are the corresponding positive $n$th roots. Hence
$$\begin{align*}(ab)^r&=(uv)^p\\(ab)^r&=u^pv^p\\(ab)^r&=a^rb^r,\\\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^r&=\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^p\\\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^r&=\frac{u^p}{v^p}\\\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^r&=\frac{a^r}{b^r}.\end{align*}$$
The integer exponents $p,q$ may be negative or zero, so these proofs include negative fractional indices and zero indices.
